summary: This informational RFC gives clear definitions of active and passive performance assessment for metrics and methods. It also defines hybrid methods that mix attributes of both, and describes dimensions along which methods can be compared.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7799 defines active and passive ways to measure network performance and names methods that combine them. It also explains how a method can affect traffic and how much its stream is known in advance.

questions: what is hybrid type i measurement
subtitle: Definitions for active, passive, and hybrid network performance measurement.

tldr.problem: The terms Active and Passive had long been used for performance measurement without precise definitions, and new methods combine their properties.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Active and Passive metrics and methods, adds two hybrid categories, and describes dimensions for evaluating measurement methods.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational terminology document that helps classify measurement methods; it specifies no protocol.

facts.label: Method categories
facts.value: Active, Passive, Hybrid Type I, Hybrid Type II

facts.label: Comparison dimensions
facts.value: Effect on network conditions; prior stream knowledge

today: RFC 7799 is an Informational document published in May 2016. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it defines measurement terminology, not a protocol.

sections.title: Active and Passive Measurement
sections.content:
An Active method depends on a dedicated packet stream created for measurement. A Passive method depends only on observing packet streams that exist whether or not measurement takes place. The RFC defines these terms more precisely and treats them as ends of a continuum.

The document also defines hybrid methods that combine Active and Passive attributes. Its purpose is to provide shared definitions and dimensions for evaluating new measurement approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: An active method creates a measurement stream. A passive method observes existing traffic without changing it.

sections.title: Active Methods and Metrics
sections.content:
Active methods generate packets, often with fields such as sequence numbers or timestamps that help identify measurements. The source and destination are usually known in advance, and the source knows the stream's characteristics. A loading stream may also be generated even if it is not measured.

Because an active test adds traffic, it can affect the conditions it measures. An Active metric includes one or more features of an Active method in its definition.
sections.plainLanguage: An active test sends packets for measurement and can identify them with dedicated fields. That extra traffic may change the network conditions being measured.

sections.title: Passive Methods and Metrics
sections.content:
A Passive method observes an undisturbed packet stream. It must not add, change, or remove packets or fields, or change field values along the path. A passive method depends on the stream being present at one or more observation points; measuring latency may require matching packets seen at several points.

Sending observations to a collector is part of a passive measurement system. That reporting traffic can affect network performance, as can management traffic from any measurement system. A Passive metric is assessed solely through observation of packet traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: A passive method watches traffic that would exist anyway and does not alter it. To measure a path, observation points may need to identify the same packets.

sections.title: Two Types of Hybrid Method
sections.content:
Hybrid Type I applies to one stream of interest when a method augments or modifies that stream, or changes how it is treated. It also includes observing an existing stream while adding a separate loading stream, because the measurement changes network conditions.

Hybrid Type II uses two or more different streams of interest with some coordination, such as Active streams together with undisturbed streams. This can support joint analysis of Active and Passive metrics. The RFC distinguishes Spatial Metrics and Methods, already defined in RFC 5644, from its Hybrid Type II category.
sections.plainLanguage: Hybrid Type I changes or adds to one stream being measured. Hybrid Type II coordinates measurements of multiple streams and combines their results.

sections.title: Comparing the Effects of Methods
sections.content:
The RFC compares methods using two dimensions: the effect of the measured stream on network conditions, and how much is known about that stream in advance. An active throughput test may add traffic and reduce throughput. A passive throughput estimate can also be low because of host or interface limits.

The RFC classifies the IPv6 Performance and Diagnostic Measurements option and packet coloring as Hybrid Type I. Ethernet loss measurement that augments user traffic is also Hybrid Type I, while synthetic loss and delay frames are Active. For security and privacy topics, it points to the LMAP framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurement methods can disturb traffic by different amounts and can start with different amounts of prior information. The chosen method can therefore affect the result.
